messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how you could use the two tools you described to place a McDonald’s order for a burger and fries. (You can adapt the steps to whatever concrete APIs you discover.) --- ## 1. Find the right API | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **1.1** | Use the *search‑internet* tool to look for “McDonald’s ordering API”, “McDonald’s menu API”, “McDonald’s place order”, “McDonald’s API documentation”, “McDonald’s API endpoint”, etc. | You need to locate the official or third‑party API that lets you query the menu, add items to a cart, and submit an order. | | **1.2** | If McDonald’s doesn’t expose a public API, broaden the search to “food‑delivery API”, “DoorDash API”, “UberEats API”, “Grubhub API”, etc. | Many restaurants rely on delivery platforms; those platforms usually have APIs you can use. | | **1.3** | Once you find a candidate API, inspect its documentation for:
• Authentication requirements (API key, OAuth, etc.)
• Endpoints for menu lookup, cart creation, checkout
• Required request payload structure
• Rate limits / usage policies | You’ll need this information to build a valid request later. | --- ## 2. Gather credentials & prerequisites | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **2.1** | Register for an account on the platform (McDonald’s, DoorDash, etc.) if required. | Some APIs require a developer account or an API key. | | **2.2** | Obtain any necessary tokens or keys. | These will be used in the `Authorization` header or as a query parameter. | | **2.3** | Determine your delivery address or store location. | The API will need a location to calculate delivery fees, availability, and to route the order. | | **2.4** | Have a payment method ready (credit card, PayPal, etc.). | The API will need a payment token or reference. | --- ## 3. Build the request payload | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **3.1** | Query the menu endpoint to get the IDs for the burger and fries you want. | The API usually requires numeric or string IDs rather than plain text names. | | **3.2** | Construct a “cart” or “order” object that includes:
• Item IDs
• Quantities
• Any customizations (e.g., extra cheese)
• Delivery address
• Payment token | This is the body that will be sent to the checkout endpoint. | | **3.3** | Format the payload as JSON (or whatever format the API expects). | Most modern APIs use JSON. | --- ## 4. Execute the API call | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **4.1** | Use the *execute‑API‑call* tool, passing the full request string:
``GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/menu?lat=...&lon=...``
or
``POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/order``
with headers:
``Authorization: Bearer ``
and body:
``{ "items": [...], "address": "...", "payment": "..." }`` | This sends the request to the server. | | **4.2** | Capture the response. | You’ll need to parse it to confirm success or handle errors. | --- ## 5. Verify & handle the response | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **5.1** | Check the HTTP status code (200‑299 = success). | Basic success indicator. | | **5.2** | Parse the JSON body for an `order_id`, `estimated_delivery_time`, `total_price`, etc. | These details let you confirm the order and track it. | | **5.3** | If the response indicates an error (e.g., 400, 401, 403, 500), read the error message and decide whether to retry, re‑authenticate, or abort. | Proper error handling ensures reliability. | --- ## 6. Optional: Post‑order actions | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **6.1** | If the API supports it, set up a webhook or polling endpoint to receive updates (e.g., “order accepted”, “out for delivery”). | Keeps you informed without manual checks. | | **6.2** | Store the `order_id` and related data in your system for future reference or analytics. | Useful for tracking, refunds, or loyalty programs. | --- ## 7. Wrap‑up 1. **Search** → **Authenticate** → **Build payload** → **Execute** → **Verify** → **Track**. 2. Keep an eye on rate limits and usage quotas. 3. If you hit a wall (no public API, no docs, etc.), consider using a third‑party service that aggregates restaurant APIs (e.g., OpenTable, Grubhub, or a custom scraper). That’s the general workflow. Once you have the concrete API details (endpoint URLs, auth method, payload schema), you can plug them into the *execute‑API‑call* tool and actually place the order.
